blocks.text: The Shifting lesson ended with a promise: once you can slide a column up or down with shift, the next natural step is turning that slid column into something a model can actually learn from. This lesson is that step. A lag feature is nothing more exotic than yesterday's value sitting in a brand new column right next to today's row, so that when a model looks at today's row it can literally see what happened the day before, the week before, or the month before, as an ordinary input column.
1. Introduction

blocks.alt: A past value becomes today's row as a lag feature

blocks.text: You already know the mechanic. shift(1) pulls the previous row's value forward, shift(-1) pulls the next row's value backward, and the index never moves while it happens. That was the entire point of the last lesson. This lesson does not repeat any of that. Instead it asks a much more practical question: once you have a shifted column sitting there, what do you actually do with it to make a model better at predicting a time series?

The answer, it turns out, is one of the highest leverage moves in all of time series machine learning. A single well chosen lag column can outperform an entire pile of cleverly engineered features, because it hands the model a piece of information that is often unreasonably predictive on its own: what this exact series was doing recently.

blocks.text: 2. What a Lag Feature Actually Is

blocks.alt: Yesterday's value becomes a column on today's row

blocks.text: Strip away the terminology and a lag feature is a simple idea wearing a slightly intimidating name. Take a column, shift it by some number of periods so it holds a past value, and keep that shifted column around permanently as one of the inputs you hand to a model. That is the whole definition. Everything else in this lesson is about doing that well instead of doing it carelessly.
2.1 A Past Value Sitting Next to the Current Row

Imagine a table of daily sales with one row per day. Right now, each row only knows about itself: today's date and today's sales figure. A lag feature adds a second number to that same row, yesterday's sales figure, computed once with shift and then stored as an ordinary column called something like lag_1. Nothing about the row's identity changes. It just knows more than it used to.

code.content:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({'sales': [200, 210, 205, 215, 230]})
df['lag_1'] = df['sales'].shift(1)
print(df)
#    sales  lag_1
# 0    200    NaN
# 1    210  200.0
# 2    205  210.0
# 3    215  205.0
# 4    230  215.0

blocks.title: This is the same shift you already know
blocks.content: There is no new mechanic here. lag_1 is just df['sales'].shift(1) given a permanent name and a permanent seat in the DataFrame, because you intend to feed it to a model rather than use it once and discard it.

blocks.text: 2.2 Why This Counts as Real Feature Engineering

In the previous lesson, a shifted column was mostly a stepping stone, something you subtracted from the original column to get a change or a percent change. Here the shifted column is the finished product. It does not get consumed by another calculation, it gets handed straight to a model as an input, sitting alongside whatever other features you have built. That shift from stepping stone to finished input is the entire difference between shift as a mechanic and lag features as a technique.
3. Why Lag Features Are So Predictive

blocks.alt: Recent history genuinely predicts what comes next

blocks.text: Here is the part that surprises people who are new to time series work. Lag features are not just one option among many equally good engineered features. For a huge share of real world time series problems, a lag feature is by a wide margin the most predictive input you can hand a model, more predictive than calendar features, rolling averages, or almost anything else you might invent.
3.1 Momentum in Real World Time Series

The reason is momentum. A staggering number of real phenomena that people try to forecast do not change randomly from one moment to the next. They drift. Today tends to resemble yesterday. This week tends to resemble last week. A quantity that was high yesterday is more likely than not to still be high today, and a quantity that was low tends to stay low, at least for a while. That tendency has a name, autocorrelation, and it is covered formally in the next section, but the intuition comes first.

items: Sales figures, a busy store today is usually still busy tomorrow, not empty
Stock prices, a stock that closed higher today has some tendency to keep drifting in that direction short term
Temperature, a hot day is almost always followed by another warm day, not a sudden freeze
Website traffic, a page that is trending today is very likely still trending tomorrow

blocks.text: 3.2 Why This Often Beats Other Engineered Features

Compare a lag feature to something like a day of week flag or a rolling average. Those features describe general patterns that apply to every row of a certain type. A lag feature describes this specific row's own immediate history, which is a far sharper, far more individualized signal. It is quite common, once you check feature importance on a trained model, to find that lag_1 alone outranks every other feature in the dataset combined.

blocks.title: Predictive does not mean magical
blocks.content: A lag feature is powerful because most real series have genuine momentum. It is not powerful because of some trick, it works because the past genuinely tends to resemble the near future for a lot of real world data. Section 6 covers the one way people accidentally make this power look even bigger than it really is.

blocks.text: 4. Building Several Lag Distances at Once

blocks.alt: Lag 1, lag 7, and lag 30 together form multiple lag features

blocks.text: A single lag column is a good start, but it is rarely the end of the story. Real forecasting problems usually benefit from looking back at several different distances at the same time, not just one, because different distances tend to capture different kinds of pattern.
4.1 lag_1, lag_7, and lag_30 as Separate Columns

Nothing stops you from calling shift several times on the same source column, with a different number of periods each time, and storing each result under its own name. The result is a handful of brand new columns, each one a different snapshot of the same series' past.

code.content:
df['lag_1'] = df['sales'].shift(1)    # yesterday
df['lag_7'] = df['sales'].shift(7)    # one week ago, same weekday
df['lag_30'] = df['sales'].shift(30)  # roughly one month ago

blocks.text: 4.2 Why a Model Benefits From Several Distances

Each lag distance tends to capture a genuinely different pattern. lag_1 captures short term momentum, what happened right before this row. lag_7 captures weekly seasonality, what this exact day of the week looked like last week, which matters enormously for anything with a Monday through Sunday rhythm. lag_30 captures a slower, longer running trend. Rather than you guessing which single distance matters most, you hand the model all three and let it decide how much weight each one deserves.

blocks.title: More lags is not automatically better
blocks.content: Adding lag_1 through lag_30 as thirty separate columns sounds thorough, but most of those distances add noise rather than signal, and every one of them costs you rows at the start of the dataset to NaN. A handful of deliberately chosen distances, picked with a reason, almost always beats a large unfocused pile.

blocks.text: 5. Autocorrelation: The Idea Behind Why This Works

Momentum is the intuitive explanation for why lag features work. Autocorrelation is the precise, measurable version of that same idea, and it is worth knowing by name because it turns guessing into checking.
5.1 What Autocorrelation Actually Measures

Autocorrelation asks a very specific question: how correlated is a series with a lagged, shifted version of itself? Take the sales column, shift it by some number of periods to get a past version of the same series, and then measure the ordinary correlation between the original column and that shifted copy. A high correlation means the series really does resemble its own past at that particular distance. A correlation near zero means it does not, and a lag feature built at that distance is unlikely to help much.
5.2 Measuring It With pandas autocorr

Pandas gives you this directly, no manual shifting and correlating required. Series.autocorr(lag=k) shifts the series by k periods internally and returns the correlation between the original and the shifted copy as a single number between minus one and one, exactly like a regular correlation coefficient.

code.content:
import pandas as pd

sales = pd.Series([200, 210, 205, 215, 230, 260, 150,
                    205, 215, 210, 220, 235, 265, 155])

print(sales.autocorr(lag=1))
# 0.15  -- weak, day to day values swing a lot around the weekend

print(sales.autocorr(lag=7))
# 0.97  -- very strong, the same weekday tends to repeat almost exactly

blocks.title: Read autocorr like any correlation number
blocks.content: Close to 1 means strongly and positively related, close to 0 means essentially unrelated, and negative values mean the series tends to move in the opposite direction at that lag. There is no single universal cutoff for what counts as high enough, but values well above roughly 0.5 are generally worth paying attention to.

blocks.text: 5.3 Letting Autocorrelation Justify a Lag Choice

This is the practical payoff. Instead of picking lag_1, lag_7, and lag_30 purely on instinct, check the autocorrelation at each candidate distance first. A high autocorrelation at a given lag is a genuinely useful signal that this specific lag distance is likely to make a good feature. A low one tells you that particular distance probably is not worth the column it would occupy. This turns lag selection from a guess into a measurement.

blocks.title: Worth checking, not a guarantee
blocks.content: A high autocorrelation is strong practical evidence, not a formal proof that a lag will help every model. Still, checking it costs one line of code, and skipping it means choosing your most important features by hunch alone.

blocks.text: 6. Lookahead Bias: The Mistake That Matters Most Here

blocks.alt: Using a future value as a lag feature is lookahead bias

blocks.text: Everything above this section describes lag features done correctly. This section describes the single most dangerous way to get them wrong, and it deserves more attention than anything else in this lesson, because it is the kind of mistake that does not announce itself. It quietly makes your model look brilliant during testing and then fails you the moment it meets the real world.

blocks.title: The one thing to remember from this entire lesson
blocks.content: If a time series model performs unrealistically well during validation, before you celebrate, check whether any feature accidentally used information from the future. That single habit will save you more pain than almost anything else in this course.

blocks.text: 6.1 What Lookahead Bias Actually Is

Lookahead bias happens when a feature on a given row accidentally contains information that, in the real world, would not exist yet at the moment you needed to make that row's prediction. The row is dated today, but one of its inputs secretly knows something about tomorrow. A model trained on features like that learns to lean on information it will never actually have available once it is deployed and making real predictions about a future that has not happened yet.
6.2 How It Creeps Into Lag Features Specifically

There are two very common ways this happens with lag features. The first is a simple sign mistake: calling shift(-1) when building what is supposed to be a genuine predictive feature. shift(-1) pulls a value from the row after the current one, which means the feature is quite literally tomorrow's value sitting on today's row. That is not a lag feature at all, it is a leak wearing a lag feature's name.

code.content:
# WRONG for a predictive feature: this pulls TOMORROW's sales onto today's row
df['not_actually_a_lag'] = df['sales'].shift(-1)

# RIGHT: this pulls YESTERDAY's sales onto today's row
df['lag_1'] = df['sales'].shift(1)

blocks.text: The second common way is more subtle and has nothing to do with shift's sign at all: shuffling a time series dataset before splitting it into training and test sets. Time series data has a natural order, and shuffling destroys it. Once the order is gone, rows that genuinely come from the future can land in your training set right alongside, or even before, rows from the past that you are trying to predict.
6.3 Why It Looks Great in Testing and Fails in Production

Here is what makes lookahead bias so dangerous: it does not cause obvious errors. It causes suspiciously good ones. A model trained with leaked future information gets to essentially peek at the answer during training, so its validation accuracy looks fantastic, sometimes almost too good to be true. The trouble only shows up later, in real production, where genuine future data simply does not exist yet at prediction time. The model that looked brilliant on your test set now has none of the information it secretly relied on, and its real world performance collapses.
6.4 How to Actually Avoid It

Two rules cover almost every case. First, when you are building a lag feature meant for real world prediction, always shift by a positive number of periods, pointing at the past. Never use a negative shift to build a feature that is supposed to predict the future, negative shift belongs to computing things like next period's target, not to inputs. Second, always keep your time series data in chronological order, and never shuffle it randomly before a train and test split. The upcoming Dataset Splitting lesson goes into this in full detail, but the short version you need right now is simple: time series splits should always cut the data at a point in time, everything before the cut for training, everything after for testing, never a random shuffle.

items: Always shift by a positive number of periods when the result is meant to be a real predictive feature
Never shuffle time series rows before splitting into train and test sets, always split at a point in time

blocks.content: This lesson only covers the feature engineering half of the lookahead bias problem. The Dataset Splitting lesson later in this course covers the other half in depth: how to split time series data correctly so that training never sees anything that happened after the point you are testing on.

blocks.text: 7. The NaN Rows Lag Features Leave Behind

blocks.alt: The earliest rows have no past value, leaving NaN

blocks.text: You already know from the Shifting lesson that shift always leaves a NaN behind at one boundary, because there is nothing to pull from past the edge of the data. Lag features inherit that exact same problem, and it is worth calling out specifically in a feature engineering context, because what you do about it now directly affects what your model gets trained on.
7.1 Why the Leading Rows Are Empty

A lag_1 column has no valid value on the very first row, because there is no row before it to look back at. A lag_7 column has no valid value on the first seven rows, for the exact same reason, just seven rows deep instead of one. The further back a lag reaches, the more leading rows it wipes out. This is not something to fix with cleverness, it is simply a fact about the start of any series: there is no past for the first few rows, because they are the past.
7.2 Drop Them, Do Not Impute Them

The Handling Missing Values lesson covered dropna and fillna as the two general tools for NaN, and both are technically available here too. In practice, though, the leading rows of a lag feature are almost always dropped outright rather than filled in. Filling lag_1's first row with a mean or a zero would mean inventing a fake past value for a day that genuinely has no history, and handing the model a number that looks like real history when it is not is itself a subtle form of the same lookahead adjacent problem from section 6, information that should not exist being presented to the model as if it were real.

code.content:
df['lag_1'] = df['sales'].shift(1)
df['lag_7'] = df['sales'].shift(7)

# drop any row missing a value in either lag column
df_clean = df.dropna(subset=['lag_1', 'lag_7'])

blocks.title: A small, deliberate, one time cost
blocks.content: Dropping the leading rows costs you a handful of rows once, right at the start of the dataset. That is a small, honest price. Inventing values to avoid paying it introduces a distortion that follows the model into every single prediction it makes afterward.

blocks.text: 8. Worked Example: lag_1 and lag_7 Sales Features

Time to put the whole lesson together on one small, continuous example: a two week run of daily sales, engineering lag_1 and lag_7, checking whether autocorrelation actually justifies those two choices, and cleaning up the leading NaN rows before the data is fit to train anything.
8.1 Setting Up Daily Sales Data
Fourteen days of sales, with a clear weekly rhythm baked in on purpose: Saturdays run high, Sundays run low, and the whole series drifts gently upward from week one to week two.

code.content:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({
    'date': pd.date_range('2024-01-01', periods=14, freq='D'),
    'sales': [200, 210, 205, 215, 230, 260, 150,
              205, 215, 210, 220, 235, 265, 155],
})
df = df.set_index('date')
print(df.head())

blocks.text: 8.2 Engineering lag_1 and lag_7
Two new columns, each one a straightforward shift of the same sales column, just at a different distance.
8.3 Checking Autocorrelation to Justify the Choice
Before trusting either column, check whether the data actually backs up the choice of one day and seven days as useful distances.

The lag_7 autocorrelation is extremely high, which makes sense given how strongly Saturdays and Sundays repeat their own pattern week to week. The lag_1 autocorrelation is much weaker, day to day sales swing a lot because of the weekend spike and dip, but it is still worth including as a baseline short term signal. Checking the numbers, rather than assuming both lags matter equally, is exactly what section 5.3 was describing.
8.4 Dropping the Leading NaN Rows Before Training

lag_1 leaves one leading NaN, lag_7 leaves seven. Once both columns exist, the rows that are actually usable for training are only the rows where every feature column has a real value, which here means the first seven rows have to go.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Column","Leading NaN Rows","Rows Remaining After dropna"],"rows":[["lag_1","1","13"],["lag_7","7","7"],["Combined subset of both","7 (the larger of the two)","7"]]}

blocks.title: The wider lag always sets the cost
blocks.content: Whenever you combine several lag distances in one dataset, the widest lag decides how many leading rows get dropped, because dropna on a subset removes any row missing even one of the columns you listed. Fourteen days of data shrinks to seven usable rows here, purely because lag_7 needed a full week of history before it had anything real to report.

blocks.text: 9. Summary and What Comes Next

blocks.alt: Lag features are covered here, rolling statistics come next

blocks.text: A lag feature turns the shift mechanic from the previous lesson into one of the most reliably useful tools in time series machine learning. It works because real world series tend to have momentum, and it can be measured and justified with autocorrelation rather than guessed at. The one thing to carry forward above everything else is the lookahead bias warning from section 6: a model that looks unbelievably good during testing is worth a second look before you trust it.

items: a lag feature is a past value of a column, stored as a brand new column, so a model can see it as an ordinary input
lag features are often extraordinarily predictive because real time series tend to have momentum, tomorrow tends to look like today
building several lag distances at once, lag_1, lag_7, lag_30, lets a model draw on short term, weekly, and longer term patterns together
autocorrelation, measured directly with Series.autocorr(lag=k), tells you whether a specific lag distance is genuinely worth engineering
lookahead bias, using future information on an earlier row, produces suspiciously good validation results followed by real world failure
always shift by a positive lag pointing at the past, and never shuffle time series data before a train and test split
the leading NaN rows a lag feature creates get dropped, not imputed, since a fabricated past value reintroduces the same kind of bias
